newsitem.title: USA: SEC sues looter of Towers estate.
newsitem.headline: SEC sues looter of Towers estate.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The businessman who was supposed to help thousands of victims defrauded by bankrupt Towers Financial Corp. was sued Thursday by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which accused him of cheating the same investors.

The civil lawsuit, filed in federal court in Manhattan, accused John Hall of Malibu, Calif., who was chairman and general partner of Qualis Care L.P., and an associate, Joel Ciniero, of running a complex scheme to obtain and loot Towers' assets during its bankruptcy proceedings.
The lawsuit also accused a third defendant, Mark Keckeisen, of aiding in the fraud. The SEC said Keckeisen has agreed to settle the civil suit without admitting or denying the allegations.
All three defendants have pleaded guilty to related criminal charges.
The lawsuit seeks repayment of illegal profits plus interest and unspecified penalties.
In March 1994, Hall formed Qualis as a joint venture to take over the failed Towers health care financing and bill collection business.

Hall's plan to take over Towers' assets was approved by a bankruptcy trustee in 1994, two years after Hall reached a settlement with securities regulators who accused him of looting a small money market fund.
In 1987, he settled accusations by bank regulators that he abused his position at a failed California bank and in 1978 he was convicted of lying to obtain a government loan.

Towers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection from creditors in 1993 after it was found that the company's former owner, Steven Hoffenberg, used it to operate what prosecutors say was the largest Ponzi scheme in history.

Hoffenberg, who drew national attention when he offered to rescue the New York Post in January 1993, pleaded guilty to conspiracy and fraud charges in April 1995. He later tried to withdraw the plea, claiming he was mentally unfit when he admitted huge frauds. A federal judge denied the request.
Hoffenberg sold more than $450 million in fraudulent notes and bonds to investors and used some of the money he collected from later investors to pay interest owed the earlier ones.

The rest of the money was used to run the Post for a short time and to operate his financial empire with inflated revenues and bogus profits that made it appear to be a major health care financing company.
After Towers filed for bankruptcy, Hall proposed a business plan calling for a partnership with Towers to increase its remaining assets by improving its health care finance business.
The hope was that this would allow Towers' 6,000 creditors to ultimately collect more cash than they would have gotten from a simple liquidation of the business.
Under the plan, Hall agreed to contribute $5 million in cash to the partnership while Towers would contribute $35 million.
The bankruptcy court, acting on a motion by the trustee, approved the plan in February 1994. The trustee transferred Towers' assets to the new entity, called Qualis Care.
Federal authorities in the criminal case said Hall had no intention of transferring the $5 million and that he and the other defendants created the false appearance the contribution had been made.

Hall and the others borrowed the $5 million from an investor for one day, authorities alleged. The transfer of the $5 million allowed Hall to take control of Qualis, which in turn received the $35 million from the Towers estate.
Within hours of receiving the $35 million, Hall embezzled $5 million from Qualis to repay the investor, authorities said.
